This locational factor is magnified for rehabilitation projects requiring specialized field assembly crews, where labor mobilization and per diem costs can be substantial. Supply chain constraints and price volatility in upstream inputs such as GOES and CTC wires also directly affect regional pricing. Any fluctuations in global commodity markets can shift LPT pricing by as much as 5% to 10% over a short period, and these increases are often amplified in regions farther away from supply hubs. In summary, while base LPT costs are largely driven by unit rating and design complexity, regional factors such as transportation, labor, and supply chain stability can significantly affect final installed pricing. Strategic steps such as developing closer-to-site manufacturing and assembly hubs and expanding domestic capacity could help reduce both cost variability and project risk and enhance LPT supply chain resiliency within the United States. 1.7 Import Reliance The U.S. LPT market remains heavily reliant on imports of both finished LPTs and upstream raw material inputs, driven by limited domestic manufacturing and assembly capacity as well as constrained domestic production of critical upstream inputs such as high-quality GOES. It is estimated that roughly 80% of LPTs consumed in the United States are imported. Rapidly increasing domestic demand for LPTs is intensifying competition for the limited supply of electrical steel and other essential inputs, both from domestic production and imports. LPTs typically require an estimated 200–400 kg of GOES per MVA of transformer capacity, implying that a 100-MVA transformer may contain 20–40 metric tons of GOES. The highest grade of GOES continues to be produced exclusively by Nippon Steel in Japan and remains unavailable from any U.S. supplier. U.S. GOES producer Cleveland-Cliffs manufactures intermediate-quality grades, but these remain more expensive than Nippon Steel’s high-quality GOES and offer no efficiency advantage over imported alternatives, making them uncommon in LPT manufacturing. As a result, U.S. LPT manufacturers rely heavily on imports primarily from Japan and South Korea for both high-grade and competitively priced intermediate-grade GOES. This dependency on foreign supply creates a significant vulnerability in the transformer supply chain, as any trade disruptions, export restrictions, or shifts in global steel production capacity could directly constrain already limited U.S. transformer manufacturing output.
